narrative.text: Lists the title fragment, authors (Yuanjie Ren at MIT, Jinzheng Li and Yidi Qi at Northeastern University), affiliations, and emails for the MerLean paper on agentic autoformalization in quantum computation.

Presents the abstract for MerLean, an agentic framework that extracts mathematical statements from LaTeX, autoformalizes them into verified Lean 4 code built on Mathlib, and autoinformalizes the result back into human-readable LaTeX blueprints, achieving end-to-end formalization of 114 statements into 2,050 Lean declarations across three theoretical quantum computing papers.

Motivates autoformalization for theoretical quantum computation—where 11,891 arXiv quant-ph submissions in 2025 strain peer review—and introduces MerLean's zero-human-in-the-loop formalization and autoinformalization pipeline evaluated on one unpublished and two published quantum computing papers.

Surveys prior work on LLM autoformalization and recent MCP-enabled agentic Lean 4 proving systems (Ax-Prover, Xu and Odersky's System Capless mechanization, and Numina-Lean-Agent), distinguishing MerLean by its fully automated end-to-end formalization of entire research papers without human guidance.

Describes the MerLean architecture (Figure 1) and the first three stages of its Claude Code-based autoformalization pipeline: multi-pass structured JSON statement extraction from LaTeX, an iterative compile-fix loop up to 30 attempts augmented with lean-lsp-mcp, leansearch, and loogle, and post-compilation semantic faithfulness checking.

Explains MerLean's explicit axiom phase—which converts unresolved subgoals or missing Mathlib prerequisites into transparent axiom declarations rather than sorry—and the autoinformalization decoder that translates verified Lean 4 declarations back into an interactive leanblueprint dependency graph and a standalone LaTeX narrative without access to the original paper text.

Reports experimental evaluation of MerLean across three quantum computing papers—Balanced Product Codes (Breuckmann & Eberhardt, 2021), Fault-Tolerant Quantum Computation (Williamson & Yoder, 2024), and an unpublished Quantum Topology manuscript—formalizing all 114 statements into 2,050 Lean declarations (41,315 lines of Lean) in under 42 wall-clock hours, with compile-attempt statistics broken down by paper and statement type.

Presents qualitative observations from the MerLean experiments: common causes of 20+ compile-attempt loops (dependent type arithmetic, missing lemmas, tactic timeouts), examples of agent-discovered helper lemmas bridging implicit mathematical steps, and explicit axiom declarations in Balanced Product Codes for homological algebra machinery absent from Mathlib (Künneth formula, tensor-homology commutativity, and spectral sequences).
Section number stub introducing Section 5.1 of the Discussion chapter.

Discusses two central challenges in MerLean: handling Mathlib gaps in specialized physics domains via well-calibrated axiom declarations that avoid trivializing main theorems, and combining automated faithfulness checks with autoinformalized blueprints to prevent compiler-satisfying hallucinations.

Outlines four future applications of MerLean: acting as a research assistant that surfaces missing implicit assumptions during manuscript drafting (as demonstrated on the unpublished Quantum Topology paper), enabling machine-verified peer review, generating synthetic (natural language, Lean 4) training data flywheels, and accelerating contributions to physics libraries such as PhysLean and Lean-QuantumInfo.

Concludes the MerLean paper by summarizing its 2,050-declaration evaluation and future plans for broader mathematical domains and full-paper benchmarks, followed by the ICLR 2026 LLM usage disclosure (Claude Opus 4.5 for MerLean and Claude Code for manuscript editing) and 22 bibliographic references.
Introductory sentence and section header for Appendix A (Formalization Examples), introducing representative Lean 4 outputs from the Fault-Tolerant QC formalization.

Presents Appendix A.1's Lean 4 formalization of Theorem 2 from Williamson & Yoder (2024) (FaultToleranceTheorem), proving via upper and lower bound calc chains and omega that the spacetime fault-distance d_ST equals the code distance d when the Cheeger constant satisfies h(G) >= 1 and measurement rounds satisfy t_o - t_i >= d.

Presents Appendix A.2's agent-discovered helper lemma weight_inequality_core (proving w' - |S| + |∂S| >= min(h(G), 1) * d by case-splitting on h(G) >= 1) and Appendix A.3's Lean 4 formalization of the Künneth formula over F2 (kunnethEquiv) for Breuckmann & Eberhardt (2021), detailing the type definitions and the axiomatized cycle preservation, boundary descent, and bijectivity steps.
